adds.title: Pesantren Waria Yogyakarta: Kami hanya belajar agama (BBC Indonesia)
adds.summary: BBC Indonesia (26 February 2016) reports that on the night of Wednesday 24 February 2016 Yogyakarta's Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah — a religious school where trans women ('waria') study Islam — was closed after the hardline Front Jihad Islam (FJI) threatened to seal it, amid what the BBC describes as rising hate speech against LGBT people 'especially in Yogyakarta'. Banguntapan district head (camat) Jati Bayubroto justified the closure on the grounds the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site; founder Shinta Ratri said about 20 waria attend the weekly weekend classes, which teach ordinary Islamic instruction. The report documents a concrete, Yogyakarta-located enforcement-adjacent event against a trans institution — the first such incident this record's dossier had recorded — while showing the shutdown proceeded on administrative/religious grounds rather than an enacted regional anti-trans regulation.

adds.title: Pesantren waria di Yogyakarta ditutup sementara (Rappler Indonesia)
adds.summary: Rappler Indonesia's 25 February 2016 report details the closure meeting: on 24 February 2016 at about 20:00 WIB a two-hour meeting at the Jagalan ward office in Yogyakarta — attended by ward/residents' officials, the lurah, the local military district commander and, in the earlier 19 February session, the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief (Kapolsek) — ended with an agreement to shut the Al-Fatah waria pesantren after the Front Jihad Islam demanded it; a waria witness said an FJI leader delivered 'fiery' anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of 'Allahu Akbar' and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, calling LGBT people 'sama-sama anak bangsa' (fellow children of the nation) and saying the regional government would study the issue. It is the first documented Yogyakarta operational-pressure event for this record's dossier, concluded on administrative/community grounds without any provincial anti-trans statute being cited.

adds.title: Wajah Solidaritas Waria Yogyakarta di Tengah Pandemi (DW Indonesia)
adds.summary: DW Indonesia (21 June 2021) reports that Yogyakarta's trans women ('transpuan'/'waria') — most working as street performers or wedding make-up artists and attached to the Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah — saw earnings fall by about 60 percent during the COVID-19 pandemic and were, in DW's words, 'ignored by the government', struggling to pay rent and buy food. The article describes a 12 June 2021 aromatherapy-candle making class at the Al-Fatah pesantren in Yogyakarta run with local small business Malini.yk to teach new income skills, and says the waria kept performing despite donors refusing even masked performances. It shows the Yogyakarta waria community and pesantren operating again years after the 2016 closure, while documenting persistent economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province.

adds.title: Upington Transgender Woman Murdered in Suspected Hate Crime (MambaOnline)
adds.summary: MambaOnline (24 May 2024) reports that on the night of Wednesday 14 May 2024, 27-year-old transgender woman Jo-Ann Isaks was found dead in her burning room in Paballelo township, Upington, after a family member saw flames at about 23:00 and discovered her body — already alight — with multiple stab wounds to the upper body. ZF Mgcawu District Municipality police spokesperson Sgt Omphile Masegela confirmed a murder case had been opened, called the investigation 'at a critical stage', reported no arrests at that date, and police publicly identified the victim as 'Jonathan Isaks' — the deadnaming this record's TGEU entry also recorded. Northern Cape LGBTIQ+ district leader Jenny Sambok said the community in the ZF Mgcawu region had been shaken, providing the local community-level response this dossier cites.

adds.title: Transgender Kimberley High School Teen Murdered in Suspected Hate Crime (MambaOnline)
adds.summary: MambaOnline (13 June 2024) reports that on 1 June 2024, 18-year-old transgender learner Karabelo Pudumo — a Grade 10 student at Pescodia High School who lived with her grandparents — was stabbed to death in Kimberley, capital of the Northern Cape; a man she had been drinking with allegedly turned on her after realising she was transgender, stabbing her more than 20 times. A suspect was reportedly arrested, though MambaOnline could not verify this with authorities, and more than 300 children and community members attended a memorial service at the school. The killing is the second suspected hate-crime murder of a transgender person in the Northern Cape within a month — after Jo-Ann Isaks' 14 May death in Upington — giving this record's dossier patterning evidence beyond a single incident.

adds.title: Kimberley to Host First-Ever Northern Cape Pride (MambaOnline)
adds.summary: MambaOnline (2 November 2024) reports the inaugural Northern Cape Pride, set for 30 November 2024 at Kimberley's Galeshewe Open Air Arena under the theme 'Pride with a Purpose', featuring a morning parade, speakers and community activities, with Pride Committee member Tebogo Makwati calling it a historic moment for the province. The article also records that the province saw at least three LGBTIQ+ community members murdered in 2024: Jo-Ann Isaks (27, transgender woman, May), Karabelo Pudumo (18, transgender high school student, June) and a 50-year-old gay man, Lazarus Ikaneng Thomas (September). It documents both organised community presence and the year's third and latest killing of an LGBTIQ+ person in the Northern Cape.

adds.title: Murder of lesbian prompts Mpumalanga march against violence (GroundUp)
adds.summary: GroundUp (6 January 2020) reports that Portia Mtsweni, a 25-year-old lesbian, was found dead — half naked with stab wounds — near Zamani Primary School in Tweefontein, Mpumalanga, in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019, and that on 2 January about 800 people marched in the Thembisile Hani Local Municipality in protest, organised by Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, the ANC Women's League and others. Thembisile Hani mayor Nomsa Mtsweni called on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence. The report documents a deadly anti-LGBTIQ incident and local community mobilisation inside Mpumalanga — province-level violence data this record's dossier had not retrieved.

adds.title: 1ST MPUMALANGA GAY PRIDE A SUCCESS (MambaOnline)
adds.summary: MambaOnline (11 September 2014) reports that Mpumalanga's first LGBTI Pride march and celebration was held on Saturday 9 August 2014 in the provincial capital Nelspruit (Mbombela) under the theme 'Moving Forward, Proud, Strong & United', with around 1,000 participants marching from the SABC offices to Nelspruit Plaza and a post-parade picnic at Oorwesig Garden Park. Organiser Joy Kunene said police were 'visible and supportive' and supplied about 20 police and traffic officers to assist, and the march launched the LGBTI Mpumalanga Movement, an umbrella group for the province's LGBTI organisations. The event is direct evidence of a public, police-supported LGBTIQ+ presence in the province's capital, tempering the record's picture of exclusively hostile local institutions.

adds.title: LGBTIQ+ community speak about discrimination at police in eMbalenhle (Ridge Times)
adds.summary: Ridge Times (29 August 2026) reports that at the Pride Flag Tour held at the eMbalenhle Sasol Club on 18 August, LGBTIQ+ community members led by the Rainbow Seed Institute raised concerns about alleged discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations; participants said they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance, and one member alleged that after being sexually assaulted in eMbalenhle months earlier, an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station asked why she 'didn't fight back'. Attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation. The report, from the Secunda-area local press, documents current, province-specific LGBTIQ+ grievances about police treatment in Mpumalanga — the kind of enforcement-facing finding this record lacked.
